Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}", "version_token": "28b32bfd-c5c0-4f68-abd2-948e70c8a38d", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:40.183Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.082Z", "placement_id": "0b6c15be-6394-4b2e-80ca-660125cbee7b", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "handling-errors-and-retries" } }

input.short_description: Reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through your pipeline.
input.body:
Transforming events in flight

Once events enter a pipeline, you can reshape their structure, filter out unwanted records, and enrich them with data from external sources — all before they reach the destination. This guide covers the three main transformation patterns.

Reshaping events

A reshape transformation maps fields from the source schema into a new output schema. This is useful when your destination expects a different structure than your source provides, or when you want to rename or reorganize fields.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=reshape-transform.json|language=json|code={ "type": "reshape", "input_schema": { "customer_id": "string", "order_amount": "number", "timestamp": "string" }, "mappings": { "customer_id": "customerId", "order_amount": "totalPrice", "timestamp": "createdAt" } }}}

You can also project only a subset of fields, drop sensitive data before it reaches the destination, or flatten nested structures.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Type coercion|body_html=

Reshape transformations can perform basic type conversion: string to number, epoch milliseconds to ISO timestamp, and boolean from string "true"/"false".

}}

Filtering events

A filter transformation passes events through a condition and drops any that don't match. This prevents your destination from filling up with irrelevant records.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter-transform.json|language=json|code={ "type": "filter", "condition": { "field": "order_amount", "operator": "gte", "value": 100 } }}}

Filters support comparison operators (eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte), string operations (contains, starts_with, ends_with), and logical combinations using and, or, and not.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Filtered events are dropped|body_html=

An event that fails a filter is silently discarded — it doesn't retry, doesn't go to the dead-letter queue, and is not sent to the destination. Use filters when you're confident you want to discard non-matching records.

}}

Enriching events

An enrichment transformation fetches additional data from an external source (a database, API, or reference table) and adds it to the event payload. This is useful for adding context that the source system doesn't provide.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich-transform.json|language=json|code={ "type": "enrich", "source": { "type": "http", "url": "https://api.example.com/customers/{customer_id}", "auth": "bearer" }, "output_field": "customer_details" }}}

Enrichments extract fields from the event (like a customer ID) to look up external data, then add the response to the event before sending it downstream. If an enrichment request fails or times out, the event retries with the standard backoff policy — see Handling errors & retries for details.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Enrichment adds latency|body_html=

Every enrichment HTTP call adds network round-trip time to event processing. For high-volume pipelines, keep enrichment APIs fast or batch-request multiple records at once.

}}

Chaining transforms

You can apply multiple transforms to a single pipeline in sequence: reshape first to normalize fields, then enrich to add context, then filter to drop unwanted records before they reach the destination.

Transforms execute in the order you define them, and any error in a transform (including enrichment failures) triggers the standard retry logic. A successful transform passes its output to the next transform in the chain.

Monitoring transformations

Track the success rate and latency of each transform in your pipeline's monitoring dashboard. Filter drops are counted separately from errors so you can distinguish between discarded events (which are intentional) and actual failures (which may need attention).

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|next_label=Handling errors & retries}}

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=reshape-transform.json|language=json|code={\n "type": "reshape",\n "input_schema": {\n "customer_id": "string",\n "order_amount": "number",\n "timestamp": "string"\n },\n "mappings": {\n "customer_id": "customerId",\n "order_amount": "totalPrice",\n "timestamp": "createdAt"\n }\n}}}

You can also project only a subset of fields, drop sensitive data before it reaches the destination, or flatten nested structures.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Type coercion|body_html=Reshape transformations can perform basic type conversion: string to number, epoch milliseconds to ISO timestamp, and boolean from string "true"/"false".}}

Filtering events

A filter transformation passes events through a condition and drops any that don't match. This prevents your destination from filling up with irrelevant records.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter-transform.json|language=json|code={\n "type": "filter",\n "condition": {\n "field": "order_amount",\n "operator": "gte",\n "value": 100\n }\n}}}

Filters support comparison operators (eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte), string operations (contains, starts_with, ends_with), and logical combinations using and, or, and not.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Filtered events are dropped|body_html=An event that fails a filter is silently discarded — it doesn't retry, doesn't go to the dead-letter queue, and is not sent to the destination. Use filters when you're confident you want to discard non-matching records.}}

Enriching events

An enrichment transformation fetches additional data from an external source (a database, API, or reference table) and adds it to the event payload. This is useful for adding context that the source system doesn't provide.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich-transform.json|language=json|code={\n "type": "enrich",\n "source": {\n "type": "http",\n "url": "https://api.example.com/customers/{customer_id}",\n "auth": "bearer"\n },\n "output_field": "customer_details"\n}}}

Enrichments extract fields from the event (like a customer ID) to look up external data, then add the response to the event before sending it downstream. If an enrichment request fails or times out, the event retries with the standard backoff policy — see Handling errors & retries for details.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Enrichment adds latency|body_html=Every enrichment HTTP call adds network round-trip time to event processing. For high-volume pipelines, keep enrichment APIs fast or batch-request multiple records at once.}}

Chaining transforms

You can apply multiple transforms to a single pipeline in sequence: reshape first to normalize fields, then enrich to add context, then filter to drop unwanted records before they reach the destination.

Transforms execute in the order you define them, and any error in a transform (including enrichment failures) triggers the standard retry logic. A successful transform passes its output to the next transform in the chain.

Monitoring transformations

Track the success rate and latency of each transform in your pipeline's monitoring dashboard. Filter drops are counted separately from errors so you can distinguish between discarded events (which are intentional) and actual failures (which may need attention).

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|next_label=Handling errors & retries}}

input.body:
Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Next steps

With a source connected, follow Building your first pipeline to wire it into a full pipeline.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/2df76640-838b-4256-956e-d8a19a602241}}|prev_label=Building your first pipeline|next_href={{cms:item/c40d6d7b-d16a-47f0-979b-086c7f59f113}}|next_label=Transforming events in flight}}

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\n "retry_policy": {\n "max_attempts": 5,\n "backoff": "exponential",\n "initial_delay_ms": 1000\n }\n}}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/c40d6d7b-d16a-47f0-979b-086c7f59f113}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}
